# emendrix

> Your regulatory dependencies, with a changelog. emendrix watches EU legislation, computes provision-level diffs when it is amended, and explains what changed in plain English where every sentence cites a provision you can click.

Not legal advice: this output is machine-computed from published texts, carries no lawyer's review, and is engineering assistance only.

The record is published three ways besides these pages: as JSON files, to model clients over MCP, and as feeds. Prefer them to reading the HTML.

## The JSON API

The record this site renders, as files a program can fetch. There is no query endpoint, no account and no key: every answer is a file, and the record's files are the committed bytes of the changelogs repository, at the same relative paths as in a clone of it.

- [The JSON API](https://example.invalid/site/api/): Every change as JSON files: an index per act, one file per version, fetched with curl.
- [Root index](https://example.invalid/site/api/v1/index.json): one row per act, naming its act index
- [Catalogue](https://example.invalid/site/api/v1/catalogue.json): every watched act's names and page addresses
- [Substances](https://example.invalid/site/api/v1/substances.json): every CAS and EC number an entry in the record prints, with its page and its file; a number missing here is printed by no entry, which says nothing about the law.
- [JSON Schemas](https://example.invalid/site/api/#layout): one per document the API serves

## The MCP server

The same record, for a model: a read-only MCP server at `/mcp`, answering streamable HTTP with one
JSON response per request, with no session, no key and no account. Its eight tools are
`list_acts`, `find_provisions`, `changes_since`, `provision_history`, `get_change`, `get_event`,
`list_disputed` and `find_substance`, and its four resources `emendrix://acts`, `emendrix://acts/{act}`,
`emendrix://changes/{act}/{version}/{location}` and `emendrix://methodology`. Every result carries
the disclaimer and the file each fact was read from, with that file's `sha256`.

It decides nothing: it does not read or interpret law, cannot search law text and cannot resolve
a free reference such as `Art. 50(2)`. Name an act by its key and a provision by its canonical
location, as `list_acts` and `find_provisions` give them.

The server describes itself at `/mcp/server-card`, and the site's `/.well-known/api-catalog`
names this endpoint and the JSON API.

A client that takes a URL needs only `https://example.invalid/site/mcp`. In Claude Code:

    claude mcp add --transport http emendrix https://example.invalid/site/mcp

In a client configured by a JSON file:

    {
      "mcpServers": {
        "emendrix": {
          "type": "http",
          "url": "https://example.invalid/site/mcp"
        }
      }
    }

- [The MCP server](https://example.invalid/site/api/#mcp): Ask a model client about the record, read-only, with no key.
- [MCP server card](https://example.invalid/site/mcp/server-card): the endpoint, version and transport as JSON, for a client that configures itself

## Watch from CI

- [Example GitHub Actions workflow](https://example.invalid/site/api/#watch-in-ci): Open an issue when a provision you depend on changes.
- [Feeds](https://example.invalid/site/feeds/): Atom, one per act and one per touched provision, and OPML per act

## Optional

- [Methodology](https://example.invalid/site/methodology/): what every figure means and does not mean
- [About](https://example.invalid/site/about/): who runs this instance and what it is not
- [API catalog](https://example.invalid/site/.well-known/api-catalog): RFC 9727 linkset naming the MCP endpoint and the JSON API
- [AI catalog](https://example.invalid/site/.well-known/ai-catalog.json): AI Catalog listing the MCP server card
